name: Citrate (citrate mixture and citrate salts)
short: Case report: high blood potassium in 2 kidney-transplant recipients on a potassium citrate salt. Aluminium drugs: more absorbed (healthy men; kidney failure). Stone trials: more side-effect dropouts.
text: In a case report of two men given potassium sodium hydrogen citrate granules (a potassium-bearing citrate commonly prescribed to prevent stones) from the 9th to the 17th day after kidney transplantation, both developed acute hyperkalaemia (high blood potassium; 7.67 and 6.05 mmol/L), one with chest tightness, nausea, muscle weakness and ascending paralysis and the other with ‘weak waves on EGG’ (the abstract does not expand the abbreviation); one needed haemofiltration, the other intravenous treatment, and both potassium levels returned to normal; the authors advise close attention to blood potassium with this salt. For citrate salts taken by mouth to prevent kidney stones, a Cochrane review of seven randomised trials in 477 adults (potassium citrate, potassium-sodium citrate or potassium-magnesium citrate) found that the main side effects were upper gastrointestinal disturbance and, in one patient, a rash; gastrointestinal adverse events were more common with citrate but not significantly (risk ratio 2.55), while dropouts due to adverse events were significantly more common with citrate than control (risk ratio 4.45). A Cochrane review in children reported that, in one trial, 6 of 48 children (12.5%) receiving potassium citrate left the trial because of adverse effects, and noted that the adverse-event data were incomplete; the reviewers concluded that a substantial number of children stopped the medication because of adverse events. For the citrate mixture used to alkalise urine in gout (the abstracts do not list which citrate salts it contains), a randomised trial in 200 patients taking benzbromarone found no treatment-emergent adverse events over 12 weeks with the citrate mixture or sodium bicarbonate; kidney function (eGFR) fell with sodium bicarbonate but not with the citrate mixture, occult blood on urine analysis was found less often with the citrate mixture (24% versus 38%), and kidney stones occurred at a similar rate in both groups. In a randomised, open-label trial in 282 men starting febuxostat, adverse events were similar across the citrate mixture, tart cherry citrate mixture and sodium bicarbonate groups, and two cohort reports from one registered prospective study in men with gout taking febuxostat found no significant difference in adverse events with or without the citrate mixture. In a controlled crossover study in 8 healthy men, taking calcium citrate with aluminium hydroxide raised urinary aluminium excretion (a marker of absorption) 11.1, 8.8 and 5.3 times on 3 consecutive days compared with aluminium hydroxide alone, although plasma aluminium levels did not differ. The authors concluded that the two must not be prescribed together in patients with kidney failure. In a randomised crossover study in 8 people with chronic kidney failure not yet on dialysis, an aluminium-containing phosphate binder taken with citric acid (the acid form of citrate) markedly raised serum and urinary aluminium, whereas taken with water it raised only urinary aluminium significantly, and citric acid alone caused no change. A 2015 editorial with no abstract is titled as describing a fatal interplay of aluminium and citrate in chronic kidney failure. No other medicine interactions were named in the cited sources.
